ideas.name: From the first conference to the Convention

en.text: The First World Climate Conference (1979) called climate change an urgent world problem and set up a World Climate Programme run by WMO, UNEP and ICSU. The Toronto Conference (1988), with over 340 participants from 46 countries, called for a global framework convention; UN Resolution 43/53 called climate change "a common concern of mankind", and WMO and UNEP set up the IPCC. The IPCC First Assessment Report (1990) shaped the negotiations, and Resolution 45/212 created the INC, which met from 1991 to 1992 and produced the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC, Rio 1992). The IPCC Second Assessment Report (1996) found a discernible human influence.

ideas.name: The Kyoto Protocol and the COPs

en.text: The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 and came into force on 16 February 2005. It set mandatory targets: developed countries were to cut greenhouse gas emissions at least 5 percent below 1990 levels during 2008–2012. The Bonn Agreements (COP 6) and Marrakesh Accords (COP 7, 2001) settled rules on emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism, sinks, compliance and support to developing countries. By 2006, 189 of 191 UN members had joined the Convention and 164 the Protocol. But the USA did not ratify and countries such as China had no required cuts, so global emissions rose more than 25 percent from 1990 to 2012.

ideas.name: The Paris Agreement and cutting emissions

en.text: The Paris Agreement (2015) followed Kyoto and was adopted by virtually every nation; each sets voluntary emission targets and reports progress regularly. In mid-2017 the United States announced it would withdraw. Costa Rica, Iceland, Norway and some cities have pledged to become carbon neutral, balancing emissions with removals such as tree planting. Cutting emissions slows the greenhouse effect and warming, reduces acid rain, haze and smog, and benefits health; the first step is renewable energy and wise, efficient use of energy in a circular economy.

screens.ask: A city emits 2.0 million tonnes of CO₂ a year. Its forests and projects remove 2.0 million tonnes. What is its net emission?
screens.after: Emissions − removals = 2.0 − 2.0 = 0. That is what "carbon neutral" means.

notes.text: The book never says the INC produced the UNFCCC (adopted May 1992, signed at Rio June 1992, in force 21 March 1994), never explains "COP", and never explains the key term "Buenos Aires Plan of Action" (COP 4, 1998). These are added (marked).
p.54: COP 6 first met in The Hague (November 2000) and resumed in Bonn in July 2001; COP 2 in Geneva was in July 1996, not June.
p.55: "emissions expected to be dropped by more than 22 percent" is an outcome, not an expectation (largely from the economic collapse of former Soviet-bloc countries).

p.56: the US status is out of date (left Nov 2020, rejoined Feb 2021, announced withdrawal again Jan 2025). The book omits the Paris goal (well below 2 °C, aiming for 1.5 °C) and the term NDCs. "it trying" → "is trying"; two paragraphs are printed twice.
